record.narrative: This first round registers high-confidence, biologically motivated comparisons between measured genomic/biomarker events and dependency scores. Because more negative CRISPR scores mean stronger dependency, hypotheses for stronger dependency are assigned direction -1 and anticipate a negative exposed-minus-comparator contrast. Hypotheses for weaker dependency are assigned direction +1 and anticipate a positive contrast. The strongest priors are: KRAS mutation and KRAS dependency; BRAF V600E and BRAF dependency; EGFR amplification and EGFR dependency; ERBB2 amplification and ERBB2 dependency; TP53 loss and weaker MDM2/USP7 dependency because p53 activation mechanisms are absent when TP53 is lost; MSI-high and stronger WRN dependency, a known selective vulnerability; SMARCA4 loss and stronger SMARCA2 dependency as BAF-complex synthetic lethality; MYC amplification and stronger DHX9/RPL11 dependency due to replication stress and ribosome/translation stress; KEAP1 loss and stronger NFE2L2 dependency under an NRF2-pathway addiction hypothesis; and PIK3CA mutation as a weaker prior for STAT3 dependency. All claims are initialized as unresolved because no evidence has yet been estimated. Future appraisals will assess effect sizes against uncertainty, consider clinical relevance thresholds, and then either refine with interactions, adjust for technical covariates, extend to under-investigated outcomes such as POLR2A, TMED10, RIT1, and KIF18A, or request independent validation for well-supported claims.

The first discovery screen separates into very strong biomarker-associated dependencies and mostly null oncogene-effect hypotheses. Estimates are already signed to each hypothesis direction. H6 (MSI-high and WRN dependency) has signed estimate +0.790, 95% interval +0.760 to +0.819; with direction -1 this corresponds to a raw shift of about -0.790, a very strong increase in WRN dependency. H7 (SMARCA4 loss and SMARCA2 dependency) has signed estimate +0.784, interval +0.765 to +0.803, also a huge increase in SMARCA2 dependency. These effects far exceed any plausible 10% clinical-significance benchmark and are internally consistent with synthetic-lethal biology, so they are accepted in this dataset. H11 (TP53 loss and USP7 dependency) has signed estimate +0.802, interval +0.782 to +0.822, indicating a large reduction/weakening of USP7 dependency in TP53-loss tumors, which is biologically plausible because USP7-MDM2-p53 dependency should be attenuated when p53 is lost; I accept this discovery result but request independent validation because it is a large effect for a less conventional dependency and is worth separating from possible technical or cohort-specific artifacts. H8 (KEAP1 loss and NFE2L2 dependency) is highly significant but opposite to the anticipated direction: signed estimate -0.796, interval -0.816 to -0.776, meaning KEAP1 loss is associated with much weaker NFE2L2 dependency in this dataset. The original hypothesis is rejected, and I register a reversed hypothesis for later validation/follow-up. The EGFR amplification claim H3 is borderline: signed estimate +0.025, interval -0.0003 to +0.0507, roughly near a 10% benchmark if using overall dependency means as a rough scale, but the interval includes zero and the evidence is not robust, so it remains unresolved. The other tested hypotheses are either null or opposite and small: KRAS/BRAF/ERBB2 oncogene events, TP53 loss-MDM2, MYC amplification-DHX9/RPL11, and PIK3CA mutation-STAT3. For accepted and borderline claims, I register refinements focused on adenocarcinoma subgroups and interactions, plus new diverse hypotheses for under-investigated outcomes such as POLR2A, KIF18A, RIT1, and TMED10.

H11 now has both discovery and independent validation evidence. The discovery estimate for TP53 loss versus wild-type on USP7 dependency, already signed to the hypothesis direction +1, is +0.802 with a 95% discovery interval from +0.782 to +0.822. The independent validation estimate is +0.800 with a stricter independent interval from +0.769 to +0.832. Because direction +1 means a more positive exposed-minus-comparator difference and dependency scores are more negative for stronger dependency, this means TP53-loss tumors are strongly associated with weaker USP7 dependency in this dataset. The magnitude is very large relative to the overall USP7 score distribution and far exceeds a 10% clinical-significance scale if the mean dependency magnitude is used as a rough denominator. The validation is concordant and excludes zero even after accounting for the maximum number of validation comparisons, so the main H11 claim is accepted and the investigation can be closed for the main overall association. Follow-up subgroup and technical robustness claims remain separate.

The reversed KEAP1/NFE2L2 claim H17 is also accepted on discovery evidence. The signed estimate is +0.796 with interval +0.776 to +0.816, indicating that KEAP1 loss is associated with much weaker NFE2L2 dependency in this dataset, the opposite of the original anticipated synthetic-lethal direction. This is a highly precise, very large discovery effect, but it is not yet independently validated, so its investigation remains active. The original H8 claim is rejected and closed because the evidence consistently points away from its anticipated direction.

The current supported discoveries are therefore MSI-high association with much stronger WRN dependency, SMARCA4 loss association with much stronger SMARCA2 dependency, TP53 loss association with much weaker USP7 dependency, and KEAP1 loss association with much weaker NFE2L2 dependency. The EGFR amplification association with stronger EGFR dependency remains unresolved because the point estimate is near a roughly 10% relative shift but the interval includes zero and the lower bound is only negligibly beyond zero. Many canonical oncogene-matched dependencies are null in this dataset, including KRAS mutation/KRAS, BRAF V600E/BRAF, and ERBB2 amplification/ERBB2, although these are association claims and do not establish causality or generalizability.

Next analyses should first test whether accepted large effects are stable across biology and technical strata: adenocarcinoma interactions for MSI-high/WRN, SMARCA4 loss/SMARCA2, TP53 loss/USP7, and KEAP1 loss/NFE2L2; main effects in the Avana library stratum; and EGFR amplification in KRAS-wild-type tumors to refine the unresolved EGFR signal. These follow-ups will distinguish broadly associated biomarker effects from subgroup-specific or technical-stratum effects.

The main discoveries so far are very large biomarker associations: MSI-high is associated with much stronger WRN dependency, SMARCA4 loss with much stronger SMARCA2 dependency, TP53 loss with much weaker USP7 dependency, and KEAP1 loss with much weaker NFE2L2 dependency. The next priority is to ask whether these associations are robust rather than artifacts of histologic subtype, assay library, co-occurring genomic events, or correlated technical features. I therefore register adenocarcinoma-restricted versions of the four main accepted associations, plus an Avana-library restriction for the newly reversed KEAP1/NFE2L2 effect. I also add BAF-complex specificity checks: SMARCA4 loss association with SMARCA2 dependency among ARID1A-wild-type samples, and ARID1A loss association with SMARCA2 dependency among SMARCA4-wild-type samples. These test whether one BAF-complex biomarker carries the signal independently of the other. For the unresolved EGFR signal, I test EGFR amplification among TP53-wild-type samples because EGFR dependency may be stronger when p53 pathway alteration is absent. I also stratify the null KRAS mutation association by TP53 status to see whether an oncogene effect is masked or concentrated by co-mutational context. Finally, I register two negative-control comparisons using research_marker_e, an assigned-role-free binary marker, on WRN and USP7 in directions matching the currently accepted large effects. If this marker shows similarly large signed associations, it would caution that some strong associations could reflect cohort or technical confounding rather than biologically specific biomarker effects.

I will prioritize the highest-information comparisons now that four very large associations have emerged. First, I test whether the accepted effects are subgroup-stable within lung adenocarcinoma using interactions for MSI-high/WRN, SMARCA4-loss/SMARCA2, TP53-loss/USP7, and KEAP1-loss/NFE2L2. These interactions tell us whether the biomarker association differs in adenocarcinoma versus the remaining subtype and directly test the most plausible histologic confounder. Second, I test assay-library robustness in the Avana stratum for MSI-high/WRN, SMARCA4-loss/SMARCA2, and the reversed KEAP1-loss/NFE2L2 association. I do not include the USP7 Avana test this round because TP53-loss/USP7 already has independent validation; I will use the freed slot for other hypotheses. Third, I include a negative-control test using research_marker_e on WRN. Since the WRN effect is huge and MSI-high is relatively rare, a strong marker-control association would raise concern that large CRISPR-score associations may be driven by correlated cohort or technical structure rather than biological specificity. Fourth, I test EGFR amplification among KRAS-wild-type samples to resolve the borderline unresolved EGFR dependency signal: an EGFR-matched effect could be masked in the full sample by KRAS-mutant tumors. Fifth, I test ARID1A loss on SMARCA2 dependency as an alternative or additional BAF-complex predictor and specificity check. Finally, I add two biologically plausible exploratory outcomes: MYC amplification and POLR2A dependency, and BRCA2 loss and KIF18A dependency.

The new results strongly support assay-stratum robustness for the three unvalidated large associations while arguing against strong histologic-subtype modification. In the Avana-library stratum, MSI-high remains associated with very much stronger WRN dependency: R18 is +0.813 in the hypothesis direction, with a 95% interval from +0.778 to +0.847. This is many standard deviations relative to the WRN score distribution and far above any 10% relative benchmark. SMARCA4 loss remains associated with very much stronger SMARCA2 dependency in Avana samples: R19 is +0.776, interval +0.753 to +0.799, also extremely large. The reversed KEAP1/NFE2L2 association is similarly large in the Avana stratum: R20 is +0.796, interval +0.774 to +0.818, indicating weaker NFE2L2 dependency in KEAP1-loss tumors. These Avana-specific acceptances are not independent validation because they use the same overall data structure, but they reduce the concern that the original effects were confined to a small library subgroup.

The adenocarcinoma interaction tests are all near null. R14 through R17 are small, around 0.01-0.03 in signed units, with intervals spanning zero and mostly well below the magnitude of the main effects. These do not support additional subtype-specific interaction effects in this dataset, so the interaction claims are rejected and closed. This should be interpreted as absence of evidence for a large interaction, not proof that interactions are impossible. The large accepted main effects appear broadly associated across the dominant histology stratum.

The negative-control test is reassuring: R21 for research_marker_e on WRN is null, with a signed estimate of -0.013 and interval -0.036 to +0.010. It does not mimic the MSI-high/WRN signal. This reduces, but does not eliminate, concern that the accepted large associations are merely generic markers of hidden cohort or technical structure.

Several exploratory hypotheses remain unsupported. ARID1A loss is not associated with stronger SMARCA2 dependency in the full population: R23 is small and opposite to the anticipated direction. This supports specificity of SMARCA4 loss rather than a generic BAF-complex marker effect, although BAF independence tests H36 and H37 are still pending. MYC amplification is not meaningfully associated with POLR2A dependency: R24 is tiny. BRCA2 loss is not associated with KIF18A dependency: R25 is small and opposite to the anticipated direction. These claims are rejected and closed.

The EGFR signal remains uncertain. In KRAS-wild-type tumors, R22 is directionally supportive of stronger EGFR dependency but small: +0.016 in the signed direction, interval -0.014 to +0.046. Relative to the mean EGFR dependency magnitude, the point estimate is roughly below the 10% threshold, while the interval still admits a modest clinically meaningful effect. Therefore H30 remains unresolved. I request independent validation for H17, the reversed KEAP1/NFE2L2 association, because it is very large, biologically counterintuitive relative to the original synthetic-lethal expectation, and now supported in the Avana stratum. If validation is concordant, H17 can be accepted with independent evidence; if discordant, the reversal will be revised or withdrawn.

The validation response for H17 is decisive. H17 is the reversed KEAP1/NFE2L2 claim: KEAP1-loss tumors are predicted, by the corrected hypothesis, to have weaker NFE2L2 CRISPR dependency, corresponding to a more positive exposed-minus-comparator difference because more negative dependency scores indicate stronger dependency. The discovery evidence R8 gave a signed estimate of +0.796 with a 95% interval from +0.776 to +0.816. The independent validation R26 gives a signed estimate of +0.791 with an interval from +0.761 to +0.821 that accounts for the maximum number of validation comparisons. The two estimates are nearly identical, both intervals are very far from zero, and the effect is enormous relative to the distribution of NFE2L2 dependency scores and relative to the 10% clinical-significance benchmark. I therefore accept H17 as a supported association in this dataset and close the main H17 investigation. This should be interpreted as an association, not proof of causality or generalizable biology outside this dataset. The original synthetic-lethal expectation in H8 remains rejected; the same validation evidence is signed negative to H8's anticipated direction, reinforcing that the raw effect points toward weaker, not stronger, NFE2L2 dependency in KEAP1-loss tumors. With this validation, two very large biomarker associations are now independently supported: TP53 loss is associated with much weaker USP7 dependency (H11), and KEAP1 loss is associated with much weaker NFE2L2 dependency (H17). The accepted but not yet independently validated large associations are MSI-high with much stronger WRN dependency and SMARCA4 loss with much stronger SMARCA2 dependency. Both have enormous discovery effects and remain robust in the dominant Avana assay stratum, and the WRN signal is not mimicked by the marker-E negative control. However, their main claims should remain active until non-Avana robustness and matched marker controls are inspected. The negative findings remain informative but are dataset-specific associations: KRAS mutation was not associated with stronger KRAS dependency, BRAF V600E with BRAF, ERBB2 amplification with ERBB2, TP53 loss with stronger MDM2, PIK3CA mutation with STAT3, MYC amplification with DHX9/RPL11/POLR2A, BRCA2 loss with KIF18A, and ARID1A loss overall with SMARCA2. Adenocarcinoma interaction tests were null for the four large effects, and the WRN marker-E control was null. The EGFR amplification association remains unresolved because the point estimates are directionally consistent with stronger EGFR dependency but small and uncertain, including in KRAS-wild-type tumors. The most informative next analyses are the registered robustness and specificity checks: non-Avana strata for WRN, SMARCA2, and NFE2L2; marker-E controls for SMARCA2, NFE2L2, and USP7; BAF-complex independence tests for SMARCA4 and ARID1A loss; EGFR co-mutation refinements; and subtype main effects. If WRN and SMARCA2 remain large and controls remain null, the next appraise should request independent validation for those main associations.

The accepted set has shifted from four unresolved candidate associations to two very large validated associations (TP53 loss with much weaker USP7 dependency, and KEAP1 loss with much weaker NFE2L2 dependency) and two very large but not yet independently validated associations (MSI-high with much stronger WRN dependency, and SMARCA4 loss with much stronger SMARCA2 dependency). Before requesting independent validation for WRN and SMARCA2, I want to reduce two alternative explanations: technical stratification and nonspecific binary-marker association. The top screen batch is a strong candidate for correlated technical structure, so I register batch_a interaction tests for the two large effects that still need validation. The hypothesis is not that batch_a will differ from the complement; rather, these tests ask whether the accepted biomarker effects are stable across batch. Large signed interactions would argue for caution, while near-null interactions would support broad within-dataset stability beyond the Avana library stratum. I also register marker_F controls on WRN and SMARCA2, in the accepted dependency directions. Because research_marker_f_positive has no assigned biological role, a large association would caution that strong dependency associations in this dataset may reflect hidden correlated cohort structure rather than biomarker-specific effects; near-null results would provide matched specificity evidence alongside the pending marker_E controls.

I also broaden exploration to unresolved and underexplored outcomes. EGFR amplification remains the most interesting near-null oncogene match: it is directionally compatible with stronger EGFR dependency but does not clear the 10% relative benchmark, so I test the TP53-loss stratum. EGFR-mutant lung cancers often have TP53 alterations, and EGFR dependency may be concentrated in that co-mutational context. For KRAS, the mutation-KRAS dependency association is null, but KRAS pathway dependence may be modified by LKB1 loss; I test whether STK11 loss is associated with stronger KRAS dependency. For STAT3, PIK3CA mutation was null, so I test PTEN loss as a complementary PI3K/AKT-pathway perturbation that could activate STAT3 through broader signaling crosstalk. Finally, I add a BAF specificity/co-loss refinement: SMARCA4 loss associated with stronger SMARCA2 dependency among ARID1A-loss tumors. This tests whether the paralog dependency is stronger when another BAF-complex gene is also lost, complementing the pending SMARCA4-in-ARID1A-wild-type and ARID1A-in-SMARCA4-wild-type tests.

I selected 12 highest-value existing hypotheses for this analysis round. The main current decision problem is whether the accepted but not yet independently validated large effects -- MSI-high/stronger WRN and SMARCA4-loss/stronger SMARCA2 -- are robust to assay stratum, screen batch, and nonspecific binary-marker controls. I therefore run non-Avana robustness tests for both H43 and H44, and also include H45 for KEAP1/NFE2L2 because even though H17 is validated as a population association, a null non-Avana complement would qualify within-dataset library generalizability. I run batch_a interaction tests H49 and H50 to assess whether the WRN and SMARCA2 effects are stable across the largest screen-batch split or driven by correlated technical structure. I run marker controls H51 and H52 on WRN and SMARCA2, plus H46 marker-E on SMARCA2, because large effects on large binary role-free markers would caution that very strong CRISPR-score associations may reflect correlated cohort structure rather than biomarker-specific biology. I include H36 and H37 to test whether SMARCA4-loss prediction of stronger SMARCA2 dependency is independent of ARID1A status and whether ARID1A loss carries any signal in SMARCA4-wild-type tumors. Finally, I include H53 to test EGFR amplification in the TP53-loss stratum, because EGFR dependency remains borderline directionally positive but unresolved and may be masked in co-mutational context, and H54 as a biologically plausible broad test of STK11 loss on KRAS pathway dependency after the KRAS mutation itself was null.

The new evidence is highly favorable to the SMARCA4-loss/SMARCA2 association and generally reassuring for specificity. H44 shows a very large non-Avana-library effect: R28 is +0.801 signed, interval +0.748 to +0.853, with valid cell sizes 61 and 174. Because H44's direction is -1, this corresponds to a strongly negative raw exposed-minus-comparator difference, i.e. much stronger SMARCA2 dependency in SMARCA4-loss tumors outside the dominant Avana stratum. This is far above the 10% relative benchmark and much larger than any observed control effect. H36 is similarly informative: R35 is +0.777 signed, interval +0.756 to +0.798, in ARID1A-wild-type tumors. This supports the specificity of SMARCA4 loss rather than generic BAF-complex loss, and H37 is null: R36 is -0.003, interval -0.025 to +0.019, arguing against ARID1A loss independently predicting stronger SMARCA2 dependency in SMARCA4-wild-type tumors. H46, H51, and H52 are marker controls; R30, R33, and R34 are all near null and far from the large biomarker effects, which reduces concern that these very large associations are driven by nonspecific role-free marker association. H45 confirms that the validated KEAP1/NFE2L2 reversal is also large in non-Avana samples: R29 is +0.794, interval +0.746 to +0.842.

The WRN robustness picture is less complete. H43 failed because the non-Avana MSI-high exposed cell had only 10 observations, so it provides no usable evidence and remains unresolved/deferred. H49 WRN batch_a interaction is not decisive: R31 is +0.048 signed, interval -0.019 to +0.115. Directionally it is compatible with a somewhat stronger association in batch_a, but the interval includes zero and admits both small and clinically large effects, so it cannot close the technical question. H50 for SMARCA2 is statistically significant but in the opposite direction to the hypothesized signed claim: R32 is -0.051 signed, interval -0.095 to -0.007. This corresponds to a modestly weaker raw association in batch_a relative to its complement. I reject the specific H50 direction, but I keep it active as a small technical caveat because the interval is not negligible and it is the one result suggesting possible screen-batch heterogeneity for SMARCA2. The main effect is so large, and the non-Avana and ARID1A-wild-type estimates are so consistent, that this small opposite interaction does not currently outweigh the association; however, I registered batch-specific main-effect proposals to quantify whether the SMARCA4 effect remains large within batch_a itself.

The EGFR signal remains unresolved. H53 is directionally supportive of stronger EGFR dependency with EGFR amplification in TP53-loss tumors (R37 +0.025, interval -0.031 to +0.080), but the point estimate is borderline relative to the 10% benchmark and the interval is wide because of smaller cells. H54 STK11 loss is null for KRAS dependency. Given that H7 now has enormous main discovery evidence, Avana robustness, non-Avana robustness, ARID1A-specificity, and null marker controls, I request independent validation of H7 rather than H6. H6 remains active, but its non-Avana stratum could not be estimated and its batch interaction remains underpowered; H7 is currently the most mature unvalidated large association. The request is an independent replication of an association in this dataset, not a test of causality or generalizability beyond the supplied system.

The newly delivered validation evidence is decisive for the SMARCA4-loss association with SMARCA2 dependency and confirms the previously accepted response deadline for TP53 loss with USP7 dependency. H7 had a very large discovery effect, R7 +0.784 [0.765, 0.803], and its independent validation, R39 +0.801 [0.771, 0.830], is concordant and still enormous after accounting for the maximum number of validation comparisons. Because H7 has direction -1, these positive signed estimates correspond to raw exposed-minus-comparator differences that are strongly negative, i.e. SMARCA4-loss tumors have much stronger, more negative SMARCA2 dependency. The effect is far above the 10% clinical-significance benchmark and is many standard deviations relative to the SMARCA2 dependency distribution. I therefore accept H7 as a supported association in this dataset and close its main investigation. This remains an association, not proof of causality or generalizability beyond the supplied data.

H28 asks whether the SMARCA4-loss/SMARCA2 association is present in the dominant Avana library stratum. Discovery R19 was +0.776 [0.753, 0.799], and validation R40 was +0.796 [0.761, 0.831]. These are essentially identical in magnitude and both are clinically enormous. I therefore accept and close H28 as an assay-stratum robustness check. Together with H44, which was large in non-Avana samples, and H36, which was large in ARID1A-wild-type tumors, this argues that the SMARCA4 effect is not confined to one library stratum or to co-loss with ARID1A. H46 and H52 marker controls were near null, and H37 showed no ARID1A-loss effect in SMARCA4-wild-type tumors. This specificity pattern reduces concern that the SMARCA2 result is a generic BAF-complex or role-free-marker artifact. The remaining SMARCA2 caveat is H50: R32 is a small interaction in the opposite direction to the hypothesized signed main-effect direction, -0.051 [-0.095, -0.007]. It is much smaller than the main effect, but I keep it active and retain H58 to quantify the batch_a main effect directly.

The H11 response deadline is satisfied. Discovery R11 was +0.802 [0.782, 0.822], and validation R13 was +0.800 [0.769, 0.832]. With direction +1, this means TP53-loss tumors have raw positive exposed-minus-comparator differences, i.e. weaker USP7 dependency. The two estimates are nearly identical, both intervals are far from zero, and the effect is much larger than the 10% benchmark. I reaffirm H11 as accepted and closed. This contrasts with H5, where TP53 loss was not associated with stronger MDM2 dependency, supporting that the USP7 result is not merely a generic TP53-loss dependency effect.

The KEAP1/NFE2L2 reversal remains accepted: H17 has discovery and validation evidence showing much weaker NFE2L2 dependency in KEAP1-loss tumors, while the original synthetic-lethal direction in H8 is rejected. Thus the dataset currently supports four very large biomarker-dependency associations: TP53 loss with much weaker USP7 dependency, KEAP1 loss with much weaker NFE2L2 dependency, SMARCA4 loss with much stronger SMARCA2 dependency, and MSI-high with much stronger WRN dependency. The first three are now independently validated in some form, while the fourth remains accepted but not yet independently validated.

H6 remains the most important unresolved large claim. It has an enormous discovery effect, R6 +0.790 [0.760, 0.819], and strong Avana-stratum support, R18 +0.813 [0.778, 0.847]. Marker-E and marker-F controls were null, which supports specificity. However, the non-Avana WRN test failed because the exposed MSI-high cell had only 10 observations, and the WRN batch_a interaction is inconclusive, R31 +0.048 [-0.019, 0.115]. I therefore keep H6 active and make independent validation of H6 the next highest-value validation decision when a request becomes available. To prepare that decision, I registered batch_b WRN robustness and marker-D controls for WRN and SMARCA2, as well as marker-D controls for the two validated reversal effects. Large marker-D effects would be a red flag for nonspecific cohort or technical structure; near-null results would further strengthen the biomarker-specific interpretation.

The broad negative findings remain dataset-specific and scientifically informative. KRAS mutation was not associated with stronger KRAS dependency, STK11 loss was not associated with KRAS dependency, BRAF V600E was not associated with BRAF dependency, ERBB2 amplification was not associated with ERBB2 dependency, TP53 loss was not associated with MDM2 dependency, PIK3CA mutation was not associated with STAT3 dependency, MYC amplification was not associated with DHX9, RPL11, or POLR2A dependency, and BRCA2 loss was not associated with KIF18A dependency. ARID1A loss overall was not associated with SMARCA2 dependency, while SMARCA4 loss was strongly associated, supporting SMARCA4-specific paralog dependence. EGFR amplification remains unresolved: overall and co-mutation-stratum point estimates are often directionally compatible with stronger EGFR dependency, but they are small relative to the clinical threshold or uncertain because of limited cell sizes. EGFR should not be accepted unless a refined stratum gives a robust, clinically meaningful, and preferably validated effect.

The most informative next analyses are therefore the registered robustness and specificity checks for WRN and the remaining controls for the validated large effects: WRN batch_a and batch_b main effects, marker-D controls for WRN, SMARCA2, NFE2L2, and USP7, pending marker-E controls for USP7 and NFE2L2, BAF co-loss H56, STAT3-PTEN H55, SMARCA2 batch_a main effect H58, and EGFR/KRAS co-mutation refinements. If WRN batch-main effects and marker controls remain favorable, I will request independent validation of H6. If any role-free marker or batch main effect is unexpectedly large, I will pause acceptance of WRN and prioritize technical-confounding explanations rather than biological interpretation.

Current state: four very large associations are accepted, and three are independently validated in some form: TP53 loss with much weaker USP7 dependency, KEAP1 loss with much weaker NFE2L2 dependency, and SMARCA4 loss with much stronger SMARCA2 dependency. MSI-high with much stronger WRN dependency is accepted but remains the main large claim without validation. The next exploratory set is therefore weighted toward WRN robustness, independence of co-mutational context for the accepted effects, specificity controls, and a few biologically motivated broad tests that could still clear the clinically meaningful 10% relative benchmark.  

For WRN, I register refinements asking whether the MSI-high association survives in higher-mutation-burden tumors, in higher-Cas9-activity screens, and in KRAS-wild-type tumors. These address plausible alternatives: that the WRN effect is driven by global hypermutation rather than MSI specifically; that it is an artifact of variable CRISPR quality; or that it is concentrated in a common co-mutational lineage. They complement the pending batch and marker-D controls. If these remain large and controls remain null, they will strengthen the case for independent validation of H6.  

For SMARCA2, I test SMARCA4 loss among TP53-wild-type tumors to determine whether the effect is not simply entangled with TP53 co-loss. I also add a cross-outcome specificity control: SMARCA4 loss versus POLR2A dependency. Because POLR2A is not mechanistically tied to SMARCA4, a near-null result would support outcome-specific paralog dependence, whereas a large effect would raise concern about broader screen or cohort structure affecting SMARCA2.  

For the validated reversal effects, I test TP53-loss/USP7 and KEAP1-loss/NFE2L2 in KRAS-wild-type tumors. KRAS co-mutation is common in lung adenocarcinoma, and these tests ask whether the large associations remain when removing a frequent co-mutational driver context. I also add marker-F controls for USP7 and NFE2L2 because marker-E and marker-D controls are already registered or pending; a null marker-F result would complete a role-free marker control set for these outcomes.  

EGFR amplification remains the most interesting unresolved oncogene match. Its overall point estimate is directionally consistent with stronger EGFR dependency but small and uncertain. I register an oncogene-exclusive adenocarcinoma context, excluding KRAS mutation, BRAF V600E, and ERBB2 amplification. If EGFR dependency is driven by a cleaner driver-exclusive population, this refinement could clarify whether the small signal becomes clinically meaningful and worth validation.  

Finally, KRAS mutation itself was not associated with stronger KRAS dependency, but pathway dependence may be shaped by upstream regulators. NF1 loss activates RAS/MAPK signaling, so I register NF1 loss versus both KRAS and RIT1 dependency. These are exploratory tests of pathway-level dependence after direct KRAS-mutation and STK11-loss tests were not significant. All proposed comparisons remain dataset-specific association tests; none imply causality or external generalizability.

The selected 12 analyses are aimed first at the central remaining decision problem: whether the accepted MSI-high/WRN association is robust enough to justify independent validation. H6 currently has an enormous signed effect, but its technical and co-factor robustness is incomplete: the non-Avana stratum was unestimable, the batch_a interaction was inconclusive, and I have not yet tested direct batch main effects, Cas9-quality or mutation-burden strata, KRAS-wild-type context, or marker-D specificity. Therefore I run WRN batch_a and batch_b main effects (H57, H63), high-mutation-burden and high-Cas9-activity strata (H64, H65), KRAS-wild-type context (H66), and the marker-D control (H59). If these remain large, clinically meaningful, and marker-D is near null, the WRN association will look much stronger than the earlier partial checks and I will consider validating H6 in the next appraise. If marker-D or one of the technical/co-factor strata shows a large contradictory or attenuating effect, I will defer validation and prioritize confounding explanations.  

The second block completes marker-D controls for the other accepted very large associations: SMARCA2, NFE2L2, and USP7 (H60, H61, H62). Because research marker D has no assigned biology, a large association would raise concern that the huge dependency-score differences reflect broad correlated cohort or technical structure rather than biomarker-specific association. Near-null marker-D results would strengthen specificity of the accepted effects, especially WRN and SMARCA2.  

I also run H58, the SMARCA4-loss main effect within batch_a, because H50 showed a small opposite batch interaction (R32 -0.051 [-0.095,-0.007]) for SMARCA2. Although H7 is validated and closed, this quantifies whether the effect remains large inside the batch associated with the caveat. H67 tests SMARCA4 loss among TP53-wild-type tumors, checking that the SMARCA2 effect is not entangled with frequent TP53 co-loss. Finally, H71 is a broad unresolved candidate: EGFR amplification in driver-exclusive adenocarcinoma, excluding KRAS mutation, BRAF V600E, and ERBB2 amplification. EGFR remains unresolved overall, but if a cleaner driver-exclusive stratum shows a clinically meaningful and reasonably precise effect, it would justify follow-up. These are dataset-specific association tests; no causal or external-generalizability claim is being advanced.

The new WRN evidence strongly supports the already accepted MSI-high association and makes independent validation the highest-value next test. For H57, the signed batch_a main effect is R41 = +0.824 [0.766, 0.882]; because the hypothesis direction is -1, this corresponds to a strongly negative raw exposed-minus-comparator difference, i.e. MSI-high tumors in batch_a have much stronger WRN dependency. H63 gives a similarly large batch_b main effect, R42 = +0.789 [0.726, 0.852]. These are not small technical artifacts: they are on the order of three standard deviations of the WRN score distribution and far exceed the 10% clinical-significance benchmark under any sensible scale. H64 shows that restricting to high mutation burden does not collapse the effect, R43 = +0.775 [0.737, 0.812], which argues against a simple explanation in which MSI-high is only a proxy for global hypermutation. H65 shows that restricting to higher Cas9 activity also leaves the effect very large, R44 = +0.776 [0.728, 0.824], reducing concern that this is an artifact of weak CRISPR performance, although Cas9 activity is missing for part of the dataset and selection into measured high-activity screens cannot be fully ruled out. H66 shows that the effect is not confined to KRAS-mutant co-mutational context, R45 = +0.792 [0.759, 0.825] in KRAS-wild-type tumors. Taken with the overall estimate R6 = +0.790 and the Avana stratum R18 = +0.813, the WRN result is highly internally robust except that the non-Avana WRN stratum remains unestimable due to only 10 exposed observations in R27.  

The role-free marker-D controls are reassuring for specificity. H59 gives R46 = +0.012 [-0.011, 0.035], H60 gives R47 = +0.002 [-0.030, 0.035], H61 gives R48 = -0.001 [-0.032, 0.031], and H62 gives R49 = +0.005 [-0.027, 0.038]. These are near null and several orders smaller than the biomarker associations. I cannot exclude a very small marker-D association, but the evidence does not support marker-D as a driver of the huge WRN, SMARCA2, NFE2L2, or USP7 effects, and these controls argue against a generic role-free-marker or broad cohort-structure explanation. I therefore reject the marker-D association hypotheses and close these controls.  

The SMARCA2 batch caveat is now resolved as a technical caveat rather than a substantive challenge. H58 gives the batch_a main effect of SMARCA4 loss on SMARCA2 as R50 = +0.747 [0.709, 0.785], again enormous. This means that although the small batch_a interaction in R32 was opposite the main-effect direction, the effect within batch_a itself remains very large. I therefore close H50. H67 similarly shows that SMARCA4 loss remains strongly associated with stronger SMARCA2 dependency among TP53-wild-type tumors, R51 = +0.787 [0.766, 0.809], reducing concern that the SMARCA2 result is merely entangled with TP53 co-loss.  

The EGFR driver-exclusive refinement remains unresolved. H71 gives R52 = +0.021 [-0.017, 0.060]. The direction is consistent with stronger EGFR dependency, but the point estimate is small, the interval includes both null and modestly larger effects, and the exposed cell is modest. This is not enough to accept an EGFR dependency association. Because many EGFR stratum tests are small and uncertain, I defer H71 and do not request validation for EGFR.  

Given that WRN now has a very large overall effect, library-stratum support, both largest batch main effects, high-mutation-burden support, high-Cas9 support, KRAS-wild-type support, and null role-free marker controls, the main remaining concern is discovery multiplicity and residual confounding. An independent validation split is the best next evidence. I request independent validation of H6. This request is for replication of a dataset association only, not a claim of causality or external generalizability.

The new validation evidence closes the last major open question about the four very large biomarker-dependency associations. For H6, MSI-high versus MSI-low or MSI-negative status in dependency_WRN, independent validation gives R53 = +0.821 [0.766, 0.877] at the stricter validation alpha = 0.00385, with valid cell sizes 125 and 1875. Because H6 has direction -1, this signed positive estimate corresponds to a strongly negative raw exposed-minus-comparator difference: MSI-high tumors have substantially more negative WRN dependency scores, i.e. stronger WRN dependency. This is concordant with, and slightly larger than, the discovery estimate R6 = +0.790 [0.760, 0.819]. The validated interval is very far from zero and the magnitude is far above the task's 10% clinically significant difference benchmark; relative to the observed WRN score standard deviation (~0.263), it is roughly a three-standard-deviation effect. Combined with prior internal robustness checks—Avana-library stratum R18 +0.813, batch_a main effect R41 +0.824, batch_b main effect R42 +0.789, high-mutation-burden stratum R43 +0.775, high-Cas9 stratum R44 +0.776, KRAS-wild-type context R45 +0.792, and null marker-D/E/F controls—this supports acceptance of MSI-high as a strong dataset-specific predictor of stronger WRN dependency. I close H6. This remains an association within the supplied dataset; it is not proof of causality or external generalizability. The only residual technical gap is the non-Avana WRN stratum, which could not be estimated because the exposed cell had only 10 observations in R27; however, the independent overall validation substantially mitigates the discovery-multiplicity concern.

The H17 response deadline is satisfied. KEAP1 loss versus no KEAP1 loss in dependency_NFE2L2 remains accepted: discovery R8 = +0.796 [0.776, 0.816] and validation R26 = +0.791 [0.761, 0.821]. Direction +1 means the raw exposed-minus-comparator difference is positive, so KEAP1-loss tumors have less negative NFE2L2 scores, i.e. weaker NFE2L2 dependency. This is a robust reversal of the initially hypothesized synthetic-lethal direction in H8, which remains rejected. I reaffirm H17 as accepted and closed.

The current supported large-association set is therefore: TP53 loss predicts much weaker USP7 dependency (H11 accepted and validated); KEAP1 loss predicts much weaker NFE2L2 dependency (H17 accepted and validated; H8 rejected); SMARCA4 loss predicts much stronger SMARCA2 dependency (H7 accepted and validated, with multiple stratum and specificity controls); and MSI-high predicts much stronger WRN dependency (H6 now accepted and validated). The SMARCA2 finding is further supported by Avana stratum validation H28, non-Avana discovery R28, ARID1A-wild-type stratum R35, TP53-wild-type stratum R51, and batch_a main effect R50. Role-free marker controls for these outcomes are near null, including marker-D, marker-E, and marker-F tests for WRN and SMARCA2, and marker-D for NFE2L2 and USP7.

The scientifically important negative findings remain dataset-specific and informative: direct matched oncogene-mutation or amplification associations were generally weak or null. KRAS mutation was not associated with stronger KRAS dependency; STK11 loss was not associated with KRAS dependency; BRAF V600E was not associated with BRAF dependency; ERBB2 amplification was not associated with ERBB2 dependency; TP53 loss was not associated with stronger MDM2 dependency; PIK3CA mutation was not associated with stronger STAT3 dependency; MYC amplification was not associated with stronger DHX9, RPL11, or POLR2A dependency; and BRCA2 loss was not associated with stronger KIF18A dependency. ARID1A loss overall was not associated with stronger SMARCA2 dependency, while SMARCA4 loss was strongly associated, supporting a more SMARCA4-specific paralogous dependence pattern rather than generic BAF-complex loss.

EGFR amplification remains the main unresolved candidate among the clinically motivated oncogene-dependency hypotheses. Several EGFR comparisons are directionally consistent with stronger EGFR dependency, including the overall estimate R3 +0.025 [-0.000, 0.051], KRAS-wild-type context R22 +0.016 [-0.014, 0.046], TP53-loss context R37 +0.025 [-0.031, 0.080], and driver-exclusive adenocarcinoma refinement R52 +0.021 [-0.017, 0.060]. However, these point estimates are small relative to the accepted huge associations and often underpowered. EGFR should not be accepted unless a more informative stratum or pooled refinement yields a clinically meaningful, reasonably precise effect and preferably independent validation. Other unresolved questions include whether the accepted large effects persist in additional co-mutational or assay-quality strata, especially TP53-loss/USP7 and KEAP1-loss/NFE2L2 in KRAS-wild-type tumors, and whether cross-outcome specificity controls such as MSI-high/POLR2A and SMARCA4-loss/POLR2A are near null.

The most informative next analyses are therefore not further validation of the already validated large associations, but (1) completing specificity controls for the large effects, especially cross-outcome controls H76 MSI-high/POLR2A and H68 SMARCA4-loss/POLR2A, plus remaining marker-E/F controls for USP7 and NFE2L2; (2) testing whether the large reversal effects remain in co-mutational contexts H69 TP53-loss/USP7 in KRAS-wild-type tumors and H70 KEAP1-loss/NFE2L2 in KRAS-wild-type tumors; and (3) resolving EGFR with the registered co-mutation-stratum refinements H14, H38, H48, and related EGFR hypotheses rather than validating the weak overall EGFR signal. These analyses will better distinguish biomarker-specific associations from broader co-mutational structure, technical confounding, or underpowered small effects.

The run now has four large, internally robust, and externally within-dataset validated associations: TP53 loss with much weaker USP7 dependency, KEAP1 loss with much weaker NFE2L2 dependency, SMARCA4 loss with much stronger SMARCA2 dependency, and MSI-high with much stronger WRN dependency. The next scientific priority is not more validation of those accepted effects, but specificity, context, and broad exploration of previously under-tested outcomes. I therefore defer many small pending refinements, including the EGFR amplification strata and residual accepted-effect subgroup checks, because their existing point estimates are far below the clinically meaningful benchmark or the main effects are already accepted with supporting strata. I closed main broad oncogene nulls H1, H2, and H4 because the central questions have been answered in this dataset. The new hypotheses are designed as falsifiable specificity controls. H77 asks whether TP53 loss also weakens NFE2L2 dependency in the same way KEAP1 loss does; H78 asks whether KEAP1 loss also weakens USP7 dependency in the way TP53 loss does. Large cross-biomarker effects would suggest that the accepted reversal associations are not outcome- or pathway-specific and could reflect broader co-mutational or assay structure, whereas near-null results would strengthen the claim that TP53 loss specifically predicts USP7 dependency and KEAP1 loss specifically predicts NFE2L2 dependency. H79 extends the strong SMARCA4-loss effect to the previously under-tested TMED10 outcome; a large effect would raise concern about broader BAF-related or screen-wide dependency structure, while a null result supports TMED10 specificity and leaves SMARCA2 as the main BAF paralog-associated outcome. H80 tests CDKN2A loss versus MDM2 dependency. CDKN2A loss is a plausible p53-pathway predictor independent of direct TP53 loss, and a clinically meaningful negative raw difference, reflected here as a positive signed estimate under direction -1, would identify a new MDM2 dependency marker. I keep H68 and H76 active as complementary POLR2A specificity controls, H69 and H70 as KRAS-wild-type context checks for the reversal effects, H42 and H47 as marker-E specificity controls, H22 as the existing TMED10 marker control, and H72 as an RAS-pathway exploration of NF1 loss versus RIT1 dependency. All interpretations remain dataset-specific associations, not causal claims or generalizable biological claims.

I select twelve analyses aimed mainly at specificity and broad untested associations rather than additional validation of the four accepted large effects. First, H77 and H78 are cross-biomarker controls: TP53 loss on NFE2L2 dependency and KEAP1 loss on USP7 dependency. Large effects would challenge the outcome specificity of the accepted TP53-USP7 and KEAP1-NFE2L2 associations, while near-null results would strengthen the interpretation that these are selective associations rather than broad consequences of correlated pathway alterations. Second, H79, H68, and H76 are cross-outcome controls on under-tested dependencies: SMARCA4 loss versus TMED10 dependency, SMARCA4 loss versus POLR2A dependency, and MSI-high versus POLR2A dependency. Near-null estimates would support that the SMARCA2 and WRN effects are not generic shifts in broad essential dependency or screen structure, whereas large effects would warrant confounding investigations. Third, H42, H47, H74, and H75 complete role-free marker controls for USP7 and NFE2L2 using markers E and F, complementing the null marker-D controls. This tests whether the accepted large reversal effects are tied to assay-agnostic markers. Fourth, H80 tests CDKN2A loss versus MDM2 dependency, a plausible p53-pathway predictor independent of direct TP53 loss. Finally, H72 and H73 test NF1 loss versus RIT1 and KRAS dependency, respectively, because NF1 loss activates RAS/MAPK signaling and provides a pathway-level follow-up after direct KRAS mutation was not associated with KRAS dependency. I defer EGFR refinements and KRAS-wild-type context checks for accepted effects this round because EGFR estimates are small and the accepted effects already have strong validation and multiple stratum controls.

The new specificity controls are largely reassuring for the four accepted large associations. H77 tests whether TP53 loss also predicts weaker NFE2L2 dependency in the same way KEAP1 loss does: R54 = +0.016 [-0.025, 0.056] under a positive direction. The point estimate is small and imprecise, with no evidence of a clinically meaningful association. H78 tests whether KEAP1 loss also predicts weaker USP7 dependency: R55 = +0.009 [-0.033, 0.050], also near null. These cross-biomarker nulls support outcome specificity: TP53 loss is associated with USP7 dependency in this dataset, and KEAP1 loss is associated with NFE2L2 dependency, but neither appears to produce the opposite very large cross-outcome effect. This does not exclude small associations, but it argues against the accepted effects being generic manifestations of broad pathway co-alteration.

The cross-outcome controls are also reassuring. SMARCA4 loss is not meaningfully associated with TMED10 dependency, R56 = -0.005 [-0.025, 0.014], or POLR2A dependency, R57 = -0.005 [-0.024, 0.014]. MSI-high is not meaningfully associated with POLR2A dependency, R58 = -0.004 [-0.035, 0.028]. Because the accepted SMARCA2 and WRN effects are enormous, a generic shift in broad essential dependency or screen-wide quality would plausibly have produced large effects on TMED10 or POLR2A as well. The near-null results therefore support that the SMARCA4-loss/SMARCA2 and MSI-high/WRN associations are relatively selective in this dataset.

Role-free marker controls are consistent with specificity. Marker-E is not associated with USP7 or NFE2L2 dependency: R60 = -0.008 [-0.040, 0.025] and R61 = +0.001 [-0.031, 0.033]. Marker-F is also near null for USP7 and NFE2L2: R62 = -0.024 [-0.056, 0.009] and R63 = -0.006 [-0.038, 0.026]. These are far smaller than the accepted large biomarker effects and do not support the idea that assay-agnostic marker structure is driving the main findings. I reject and close these marker-control claims.

The NF1-loss RAS-pathway explorations are null in the claimed direction. NF1 loss is not associated with stronger RIT1 dependency, R64 = -0.021 [-0.049, 0.008], nor stronger KRAS dependency, R65 = -0.020 [-0.049, 0.009]. These are small and imprecise, and do not support a clinically meaningful dependency-marker association in this dataset. I reject and close them.

The only new non-null discovery is H80, CDKN2A loss versus MDM2 dependency. Because H80 has direction -1, the signed estimate R59 = +0.117 [0.082, 0.152] corresponds to a negative raw exposed-minus-comparator difference: CDKN2A-loss tumors have more negative MDM2 scores, i.e. stronger MDM2 dependency. The effect is not huge relative to the previously validated associations, which are around +0.8, but it is moderate, precise, and clinically meaningful by the stated threshold: it is about 0.52 standard deviations of MDM2 dependency and its interval excludes very small EGFR-like effects. The direct TP53-loss association with MDM2 was null, so CDKN2A loss may identify a p53-pathway context for MDM2 dependency through a different mechanism, possibly involving cell-cycle or co-deletion structure. Given the large number of discovery comparisons tested, I do not want to close on discovery alone, but the evidence is strong enough to accept the dataset association now while validation is run. I therefore accept H80, keep it active, and request independent validation. If validation confirms, H80 can become an additional robust predictor of stronger MDM2 dependency in this dataset. If validation fails or is unstable, I will revisit its status.

All conclusions remain dataset-specific associations, not causal claims and not claims of external generalizability.

The response-deadline validation for H7 confirms the central SMARCA4-loss association. H7 is direction -1, so the positive signed estimates mean a more negative raw exposed-minus-comparator difference, i.e. stronger SMARCA2 dependency among SMARCA4-loss tumors. Discovery R7 = +0.784 [0.765, 0.803] and independent validation R39 = +0.801 [0.771, 0.830] at the stricter validation alpha 0.00385 are concordant, large, and imprecise only at a negligible level. H28 further confirms the effect within the Avana-library stratum: discovery R19 = +0.776 [0.753, 0.799] and validation R40 = +0.796 [0.761, 0.831]. Together with non-Avana discovery R28, ARID1A-wild-type stratum R35, TP53-wild-type stratum R51, batch_a main effect R50, and near-null role-free marker controls, SMARCA4 loss as a dataset-specific predictor of much stronger SMARCA2 dependency is accepted and closed.

The new validation for H80 resolves the fifth candidate association: CDKN2A loss predicts stronger MDM2 dependency. H80 has direction -1, so the positive signed estimates correspond to a negative raw exposed-minus-comparator difference; CDKN2A-loss tumors have more negative dependency_MDM2 scores. Discovery R59 = +0.117 [0.082, 0.152] and independent validation R66 = +0.130 [0.078, 0.182] are both valid, statistically convincing under the multiplicity-adjusted validation alpha, and concordant in direction and magnitude. The validation point estimate is slightly larger than discovery, though with wider uncertainty, which is normal in a validation split. Relative to the observed MDM2 dependency standard deviation of roughly 0.226, the validation effect is about 0.57 SD. Relative to the cohort mean MDM2 dependency magnitude of about 0.27, the point estimate is roughly a 48% shift in score magnitude and the validation lower bound is roughly 29%, comfortably above the task's 10% clinical-significance benchmark. Therefore I accept H80 as a dataset-specific association and close its investigation.

This result is scientifically interesting because the direct TP53-loss predictor for MDM2 dependency was null (H5, R5 = +0.009 [-0.016, 0.034] under direction +1, rejected). CDKN2A loss may identify a different p53-pathway or cell-cycle context for MDM2 dependency, or it may be a marker of broader 9p21 deletion structure because MTAP loss frequently co-occurs with CDKN2A loss. The next most informative analyses are therefore mechanism and co-deletion controls, not further validation of H80. I registered MTAP-loss as a predictor, CDKN2A-loss effects stratified by MTAP loss, CDKN2A-loss effects stratified by TP53 loss, and an MTAP-loss interaction test. These will distinguish an MTAP/9p21 co-deletion marker from a more CDKN2A-specific association and will test whether the MDM2 effect is concentrated in TP53-wildtype biology. All current conclusions remain associations in this supplied dataset; none should be interpreted as causal or externally generalizable.

The final supported dataset association set is now: MSI-high predicts much stronger WRN dependency (H6), SMARCA4 loss predicts much stronger SMARCA2 dependency (H7), TP53 loss predicts much weaker USP7 dependency (H11), KEAP1 loss predicts much weaker NFE2L2 dependency (H17; original synthetic-lethal direction H8 rejected), and CDKN2A loss predicts stronger MDM2 dependency (H80). Major negative findings remain informative: direct oncogene or matched-dependency associations were largely null or too small, including KRAS mutation/KRAS dependency, BRAF V600E/BRAF dependency, ERBB2 amplification/ERBB2 dependency, PIK3CA/STAT3, MYC/DHX9-RPL11-POLR2A, BRCA2/KIF18A, STK11/KRAS, NF1/RIT1, and NF1/KRAS. EGFR amplification remains deferred and unresolved because multiple estimates are directionally positive but small or imprecise.

The currently supported dataset-specific associations are MSI-high with much stronger WRN dependency (H6), SMARCA4 loss with much stronger SMARCA2 dependency (H7), TP53 loss with much weaker USP7 dependency (H11), KEAP1 loss with much weaker NFE2L2 dependency (H17; the opposite synthetic-lethal direction H8 is rejected), and CDKN2A loss with stronger MDM2 dependency (H80). The newest accepted effect, CDKN2A-MDM2, now needs specificity and robustness follow-up more than additional validation. I registered role-free marker controls for MDM2 (marker D/E/F) because a clinically meaningful association between any assay-agnostic marker and MDM2 dependency would raise concern that the CDKN2A-MDM2 signal reflects dataset structure rather than genomic specificity; near-null marker effects would support biological specificity. I also registered CDKN2A-loss cross-outcome tests: USP7 with direction +1 tests whether CDKN2A loss behaves like generic p53-pathway loss by weakening USP7 dependency, whereas a null result supports selective MDM2 association; POLR2A with direction -1 tests whether CDKN2A loss produces broad essential-dependency shifts, where a near-null result supports selectivity.

I registered library robustness strata for CDKN2A-MDM2 in Avana and non-Avana screens. Concordant negative raw differences, reported as positive signed estimates under direction -1, would strengthen the interpretation that H80 is not library-specific; divergent or imprecise estimates would narrow the claim to a more context-dependent dataset association. I also tested MTAP loss among CDKN2A-intact tumors with direction -1. A clinically meaningful MTAP association independent of CDKN2A loss would support a broader 9p21 deletion or co-deletion explanation for stronger MDM2 dependency. A null result, together with the pending CDKN2A-by-MTAP strata, would favor a more CDKN2A-specific or co-deletion-dependent marker rather than MTAP alone.

For broader exploration of under-tested outcomes, I registered three biologically motivated hypotheses. RB1 loss versus KIF18A dependency tests whether RB1-pathway loss increases proliferative pressure and strengthens mitotic dependency. NF1 loss versus STAT3 dependency tests whether RAS/MAPK activation by NF1 loss increases STAT3 pathway dependency. ERBB2 amplification versus EGFR dependency tests a cross-HER-family association: ERBB2 amplification could either predict stronger EGFR dependency through HER-family signaling coupling or weaker EGFR dependency through bypass signaling, so the anticipated direction is uncertain but the hypothesis is clinically informative. Finally, I registered MSI-high versus WRN dependency within the KY library stratum to test the WRN effect outside the dominant Avana library; concordant strong WRN dependency would further support robustness, while an attenuated or imprecise estimate would identify a technical or library context limitation. All proposed tests are exploratory associations in the supplied dataset, not causal claims or externally generalizable claims.

I am selecting the twelve newly registered claims H87-H98 because they directly target the next scientific questions after accepting five dataset associations: MSI-high/WRN, SMARCA4-loss/SMARCA2, TP53-loss/USP7, KEAP1-loss/NFE2L2, and CDKN2A-loss/MDM2. The first block (H87-H89) tests whether MDM2 dependency is associated with role-free markers D, E, or F. Clinically meaningful marker associations, roughly 0.027 or larger relative to the mean MDM2 dependency magnitude, would weaken the interpretation that the CDKN2A-MDM2 signal is biologically or genomically specific and raise concern about dataset-wide marker structure. Near-null estimates would support specificity of CDKN2A loss. The next block (H90-H91) tests CDKN2A-loss cross-outcome specificity: H90 asks whether CDKN2A loss also weakens USP7 dependency, as TP53 loss does; H91 asks whether it produces a broader POLR2A essential-dependency shift. Near-null results would support a selective CDKN2A-MDM2 association rather than a generic p53-pathway or global screen-structure effect. H92-H93 test library robustness of CDKN2A-MDM2 within Avana and non-Avana screens. H94 tests MTAP loss among CDKN2A-intact tumors, distinguishing whether MTAP co-loss can explain the CDKN2A-MDM2 association or whether CDKN2A retains a more specific signal. The final block tests biologically motivated untested associations: RB1 loss versus KIF18A mitotic dependency, NF1 loss versus STAT3 dependency, ERBB2 amplification versus EGFR dependency, and MSI-high versus WRN dependency in the KY library. These add broad exploration while not reallocating analysis effort to deferred small-effect EGFR refinements or accepted-effect subgroup checks.

The new results largely strengthen the specificity and robustness of the supported associations, while leaving one borderline library stratum unresolved. For MDM2, the role-free marker controls are clinically uninformative in the claimed direction. H87 R67 = -0.0187 [-0.0385, 0.0012] under direction -1 corresponds to a raw exposed-minus-comparator difference of about +0.019, i.e. slightly weaker MDM2 dependency in marker-D-positive tumors, far below the approximate 0.027 ten-percent MDM2 threshold. Marker E (R68 = +0.0036 [-0.0163, 0.0235]) and marker F (R69 = +0.0129 [-0.0069, 0.0328]) are also near null, with observed magnitudes below the threshold and intervals containing zero. These marker nulls reduce concern that the CDKN2A-MDM2 signal is driven by assay-agnostic marker structure, although some intervals are wide enough that modest opposite-direction associations cannot be completely excluded. CDKN2A-loss cross-outcome controls also support selectivity: CDKN2A loss is not associated with weaker USP7 dependency in the claimed positive direction (R70 = -0.0023 [-0.0429, 0.0383]) and is not associated with a clinically meaningful POLR2A shift (R71 = +0.0020 [-0.0176, 0.0215]). The POLR2A interval is tight relative to the outcome threshold and is the stronger specificity evidence. Library robustness is mostly concordant. Within Avana, CDKN2A loss predicts stronger MDM2 dependency: R72 = +0.1158 [0.0785, 0.1531], a precise and clinically meaningful effect; I accept H92 and close it. In the KY library, MSI-high predicts much stronger WRN dependency: R78 = +0.7323 [0.6746, 0.7900], far above threshold; I accept H98 and close it as a robust non-Avana stratum for the WRN finding. The non-Avana CDKN2A-MDM2 stratum is more fragile: R73 = +0.1255 [0.0291, 0.2218], with only 47 exposed observations and a lower bound barely above the 0.027 threshold. The point estimate is encouraging and concordant, but the uncertainty is substantial, so I leave H93 unresolved active rather than accepting the stratum conclusively. MTAP loss among CDKN2A-intact tumors is not associated with stronger MDM2 dependency (R74 = +0.0042 [-0.0178, 0.0263]), supporting a more CDKN2A-associated signal rather than MTAP loss acting alone in intact tumors. The broader biological hypotheses are negative: RB1 loss is not clinically supported for KIF18A dependency (R75 = +0.0082 [-0.0193, 0.0357]), NF1 loss is not supported for STAT3 dependency (R76 = -0.0079 [-0.0407, 0.0248]), and ERBB2 amplification is not associated with EGFR dependency in the claimed direction (R77 = -0.0032 [-0.0296, 0.0231]). Overall, I request no new validation now: the strongest new accepted items are strata of already validated or extremely large effects, H93 is borderline and strict validation may be inconclusive, and the remaining EGFR amplification signal remains imprecise. All conclusions remain dataset-specific associations, not causal or externally generalizable claims.

The response-deadline validation for H6 confirms the MSI-high WRN association. H6 is direction -1, so the positive signed estimates correspond to a negative exposed-minus-comparator raw difference: MSI-high lines have more negative WRN dependency scores, i.e. stronger WRN dependency. Discovery R6 = +0.790 [0.760, 0.819] and independent validation R53 = +0.821 [0.766, 0.877] are concordant and enormous relative to the WRN score scale, whose mean magnitude is about 0.301 and SD about 0.263. The validation lower bound is still far above the 10% clinical threshold, so H6 remains accepted and closed. The earlier accepted strata, including Avana, KY library, batch_a, batch_b, high mutation burden, high Cas9 activity, KRAS-wildtype, and marker-null controls, make this one of the most robust dataset-specific associations in the study.

The newly delivered validation for H42 is null. H42 tests a role-free marker-E association with USP7 dependency. Discovery R60 = -0.008 [-0.040, 0.025] and validation R79 = -0.001 [-0.049, 0.046] are centered essentially at zero, with wide validation uncertainty but no sign of a meaningful association. USP7's mean score magnitude is about 0.093, and the observed estimates are orders of magnitude below a 10% clinical shift. This supports rejecting H42 and closing it as a marker-control negative. It does not undermine H11; instead, it reinforces that TP53 loss is a specific predictor of much weaker USP7 dependency, not a generic marker-correlated effect.

The supported dataset-specific association set remains: MSI-high predicts much stronger WRN dependency (H6), SMARCA4 loss predicts much stronger SMARCA2 dependency (H7), TP53 loss predicts much weaker USP7 dependency (H11), KEAP1 loss predicts much weaker NFE2L2 dependency (H17; original opposite direction H8 rejected), and CDKN2A loss predicts stronger MDM2 dependency (H80). The next most informative step is not more validation of these accepted effects but mechanism, co-alteration, and robustness characterization, especially for CDKN2A/MDM2. I registered additional refinements to test whether MTAP loss within CDKN2A-loss tumors modifies the MDM2 effect, whether CDKN2A loss remains associated with stronger MDM2 dependency when both MTAP and TP53 are intact, and whether the CDKN2A effect is concentrated in tumors with low 9p21 copy number, a proxy for larger deletion structure. I also registered a lower Cas9-activity WRN stratum as a technical robustness check for the MSI-high finding. If CDKN2A remains strong in MTAP-intact, TP53-intact, and low-deletion contexts, interpret H80 as more CDKN2A-associated. If the effect concentrates with MTAP loss or low 9p21 copy number, interpret it more as a broader 9p21 co-deletion marker. All conclusions remain associations within the supplied dataset and are not causal or externally generalizable claims.
